stories.body:
It turns out most of us no longer believe in progress. And when that happens, it quickly becomes a crisis for societies like ours

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

D epending on your politics, the monsters are everywhere. Perhaps you see them in the form of tech billionaires and the artificial intelligence they’re developing. Perhaps you see them in the bin fire of social media they bequeathed us before that, or the legacy media that refuse to tell you “the truth”. You might see them in the manosphere, or the institutions teaching our kids gender fluidity. Maybe you see them in the migrant youth wielding machetes in the suburbs, or the refugee attempting to behead someone on a Belfast street. Or perhaps you see them in the violent anti-immigrant mobs that torched houses in response. If so, you’ll likely see them in the March for Australia or the Unite the Kingdom rallies, organised by far-right groups but attended by many more besides. You’ll almost certainly see them in at least one of Hamas, Israel or those local advocates at each other’s throats over the Middle East. I suspect you’ll see them in Russia but that can no longer be assumed. And I’d guess that you’d see them in at least one political party with a significant share of the vote.

Something in that paragraph probably outraged you. In which case, you’re probably seeing monsters in whoever sees different monsters from you. It would be easy here to make a point about polarisation. But I want to look at the deep disquiet that lies underneath.

Within the commotion of our times – Trump or wokeness or Zohran Mamdani’s stunning win in New York – is a common verdict that the conventional order has failed. It cannot be reformed, or tweaked to fulfil its purpose. It is more that the promises it made have been fundamentally broken, that it is simply incapable of delivering the good life. Perhaps it never was, perhaps it can no longer – the flavour of the rejections vary but the terminus is the same. The disillusionment does not stem from the sense that we’re going through a rough patch or that conventional wisdom isn’t delivering. It’s that it can’t deliver.

Speaking to the Monthly about inflation and the cost of living, the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says “all of these rolling shocks for 20 years have been cumulative. And every time it feels like ordinary people are going to get off the mat, something else arrives.” It’s a perceptive diagnosis, but to describe things more fully it needs to acknowledge that these rolling shocks span the economic, social, political and cultural realms.

Consider even a cursory list … September 11 and the “war on terror” placed security front and centre. The 2005 London Tube bombings raised the spectre of homegrown terrorism, triggering all sorts of social anxieties. Wars in Afghanistan and especially Iraq revealed the limits of western military power and undermined trust in governments that either imagined or invented weapons of mass destruction. Then came the urgent awareness of climate change, which variously evoked existential dread and threatened to phase out entire industries on which depend economies and communities. Soon followed the global financial crisis, which caused millions around the world to lose their homes and life savings and revealed the edifice of our global economy to be more a house of cards than a cathedral. Then came Islamic State, reviving the spectre that began the century in the crudest, most brutal form. Next, Brexit and the election of Donald Trump – both previously unthinkable, both smashing all manner of orthodoxies, thrilling or terrifying according to taste.

The dust hadn’t even settled when Covid-19 arrived, shuttering economies and lives, inflicting psychological torment, radically expanding state power. It drove us into isolation and on to our phones, where we argued over lockdowns and masks and vaccines – seeding growing suspicion of authority, whether political or medical. Social media became ever more present and polarising. Covid abated but inflation took off. Then Hamas slaughtered Israeli civilians on 7 October 2023, and Israel annihilated Gaza in response with relative impunity, yielding unfathomable human suffering that ricocheted through cyberspace and into visceral local antagonism in societies around the world. Trump was re-elected and launched a trade war on the world which he called “Liberation Day”. Then, in Australia, came Bondi . And while all this was happening, artificial intelligence emerged exponentially, developing faster than we could comprehend and threatening everything from swallowing up jobs by the million to unleashing killer robots.

Broad, deep, relentless. And what matters most is the compounding effect: a near-constant sense of crisis in almost every sphere of life. It is not something likely to be finessed with policy. At a certain level, this isn’t even about policy any more. Take immigration, perhaps the issue most clearly associated with One Nation. It’s true that Pauline Hanson’s supporters think immigration is too high, but this hardly sets them apart: up to 60% of Australians agree. More instructively, in the words of Redbridge’s Simon Welsh, “there’s a massive chunk of One Nation voters that immigration isn’t particularly important to”.

“It’s not ideological, it’s not about moving right, it’s not even necessarily about policy,” Welsh says. “They’re coming across because it is the vehicle for this fury that is directed towards the major parties because of this very long sense of neglect and social economic disempowerment that has become so profound.” It’s not that this brand of politics offers no doctrines. It does, gathering around stronger borders, a bigger military, a dismissal of climate change and a rejection of political correctness. It’s just that the doctrines are not the main game. The aim is not a policy win. It’s to break the system.

There have always been those of us who think the past was better or the future will be worse. But in our lifetimes they have been the curmudgeonly exception – nostalgics and Luddites, mostly ignored while everyone else got on with things. Now they’re the majority. In their experience, the pandemic isn’t a low point in our lives, it’s merely a way station on a path of terminal decline. It turns out most of us no longer believe in progress.

When people stop believing in progress, it quickly becomes a crisis for societies like ours. Our political order was built on the promise of expanding wealth and greater control over our lives. It said we could dream big, then pursue those dreams, and that if we didn’t achieve them, maybe our children would. It assumed each generation would live longer and be more comfortable. Partisan combatants might have labelled themselves conservative or progressive, but both made this same fundamental offer. The conservative-progressive divide was mostly about the best way to deliver constant improvement and who was best equipped to do so. There might be winners or losers. There might be the odd speed bump or correction, but the direction of travel was clear.

As disillusionment sets in, there is no shortage of culprits. One possibility is to tell a story about capitalism, which generates gaping inequalities and destroys the planet. This becomes primarily a tale of economic pain and survival anxiety, which is why the roots of the populist right are in the working class. Another story blames the depredations of the internet: the torrents of misinformation and disinformation, the incessant polarisation, the unleashing of extreme hate-filled rhetoric that has us holding each other in contempt while we collectively lose our minds. There’s truth in both these accounts but I suspect they pull up short. Beneath them lies a master concept so fundamental we often don’t stop to name it: liberalism. What’s most fundamentally changing is people’s relationship with this underlying philosophy.

Liberalism defines almost our entire social and political order in the west. Much of this is institutional: a free press, an independent judiciary, the separation of powers, governments hemmed in by constitutions, the sovereignty of the people. Some of it reflects philosophical commitments: individual freedom as the foundation undergirding specific freedoms of speech, association, conscience, religion and trade; a belief that government rules by the consent of the governed and that all citizens are equal. And the overarching character of this arrangement is clear: less hierarchy, fewer hang-ups, fewer social mores, more and easier diversity. A world of choice, and ever-proliferating choices. And, taxes aside, it’s progress without sacrifice or serious restraint. Each individual person pursuing their individual dream would make life better overall.

The various modes of upheaval we’re seeing – conservative, progressive, victorious and vanquished – are all reactions to liberalism, often explicitly. Understanding them all as “post-liberal” allows us to make at least some sense of the chaos we’re seeing. It also helps us assess whether and to what extent liberalism now finds itself in a state of disrepair. Post-liberal thinkers clearly think that case is closed. Occasionally, they declare liberalism – the old world – not merely dying but already dead. I’m not convinced of that. But I do think liberalism is in trouble for reasons it often fails to understand.

Normally, the term “post-liberal” is applied to conservatives, because many conservative critics of liberalism have themselves used and embraced the term – think the US vice-president, JD Vance. And while woke politics comes from a different place again – a radical strand of postmodernism – it attacks liberalism’s tensions and contradictions no less stridently. That is why we experience several of these movements as radical. Monsters, if you like. That’s why it probably feels like the world is ending. But if anything is ending, it’s a particular version of the world that has broadly held sway in western democracies since the end of the second world war and had been developing for centuries.

stories.body:
MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspective

U ntil now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot , and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened.

But underneath the sense of relief that many Labour MPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality.

In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict.

This week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash.

It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre.

Among the more experienced hands in government, there is a firm view that the new administration cannot return to the days of slim headroom given Reeves’s experience last year, which led to more brutal proposed welfare cuts and ultimately a backbench rebellion last summer.

Healey has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in North Carolina and is acutely conscious of factors beyond his control that will hit the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, including the rising cost of oil after bombing resumed in Iran.

It is little surprise, then, that he has repeatedly stressed that fiscal responsibility is the “bedrock” of his approach and he will stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules.

But his cautious tone jars uncomfortably with the prime minister’s large – and costly – policy vision: more public control of utilities, reform of the broken social care system and a mass social home building programme.

“[Healey] is in a bind,” one Treasury source said. “His instinct is to keep things steady, especially while the OBR does its snapshot, but that’s not Andy’s gameplan for his first week back.”

Indeed, Downing Street has been eager to ensure Burnham’s vision stays front and centre. In a mammoth three-and-a-half-hour Commons session on Tuesday, he repeatedly promised to deliver the “much more substantial change” the country was crying out for.

Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been some mutterings that Healey could, like chancellors before him, be in danger of being “captured” by the Treasury and its more orthodox arguments. “John did not exactly show in the Ministry of Defence that he was good at questioning internal departmental wisdom and pressures,” one government aide said.

The friction between the two operations burst into the open last week when Healey suggested in a television interview that Burnham was running a “continuity” government.

No 10 insiders pushed back hard. “Nobody listening to Andy and his plans for growth could think he is just about continuity,” said one senior figure. “He’s going to change things.”

A timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Burnham’s biggest legacies – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend.

Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”.

Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs.

after newsletter promotion

While not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central growth argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold.

The chancellor has privately acknowledged there is room for modest additional borrowing to fund investment given Reeves’s rule change in 2024, which allowed the Treasury to offset financial assets against government debt.

However, there is little sense of a radical new perspective emerging from the new regime at No 11. On Monday, Healey will give a speech on the government’s mission for growth, which is expected to stress the importance of devolution and public investment – both themes Reeves repeatedly returned to.

The chancellor will emphasise the need to give the private sector the confidence to invest – raising doubts about whether he is likely to go ahead with one of the big revenue raisers that progressive economists and the TUC have called for: a windfall tax on banks.

Treasury sources have declined to say whether Healey will stick to Reeves’s intention of holding only one major “fiscal event” each year, with the spring forecast a much more low-key affair. That would leave open the possibility of using his 28 October statement to fund the gaps in the defence investment plan and make more progress on tax devolution, while leaving the weightier tax and spending decisions until the spring.

Labour MPs are anxious for change as quickly as the government can deliver it. They applaud Burnham’s ambition and the sense of hope he fosters but worry that the economic realities will drag him down.

Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, summed up the mood when he suggested at PMQs that “vibes alone just will not be enough”. While he was referring to military spending, the sentiment is shared across the backbenches.

Burnham has repeatedly said he will be relentless in fulfilling his priorities. But some of his MPs are already worried that his promise to repair the crumbling state and offer “breathing space” on the cost of living could be hard to reconcile with promises of fiscal responsibility.

Downing Street sources argue, however, that it is only by improving infrastructure and devolving power that the British economy can grow as fast as Manchester’s. They cite Burnham’s visit to Cornwall this summer, where businesses told him it was taking them a year to connect to the grid.

Healey’s economic instincts are less clear. When asked what would be the main difference between him and his instinctively prudent predecessor, one adviser said: “To be honest, I think he will actually be more cautious.”

Despite his apparent wariness, government aides insist the chancellor is fully onboard with Burnham’s vision. One said: “There will always be tensions between the different parts of government, but John is aligned with Andy’s agenda. And he knows who is boss.”

stories.title: Richard Alston, trailblazer and guiding light of British dance, dies aged 77
stories.summary: Akram Khan among those paying tribute to ‘pioneering’ choreographer of intense musicality and grace who inspired generations of dancers Sir Richard Alston, the British choreographer and teacher who took contemporary dance into new directions with his elegant and intelligent creations, has died at the age of 77. A former artistic director of Rambert and the Place, where he made more than 50 pieces for the Richard Alston Dance Company , he was celebrated for lucid, emotionally attuned work that was often as graceful as it was rigorous. His death was announced on Monday by the Richard Alston Foundation , which was established in 2021 to promote contemporary dance and preserve his work. “It is with deep sadness that we have to report the death of Sir Richard Alston,” said the statement . “After a period of ill-health, and despite exceptional treatment at the Royal Free Hospital in Hampstead and the support of his closest friends, he passed away peacefully at his home on 7 September. While Richard is best known for his extraordinary career and contribution to contemporary dance, we will also remember him for his wit, warmth and generosity of spirit.” Continue reading...
